content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a novel CNN-based architecture for Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) to solve the pathfinding problem in the maze, which could realize the basic algorithms for graph, Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS). By recursively applying hand-code CNN layer to the square-size maze map,  NCA could implement Dijkstra map generation and path extraction, which are the key components for BFS and DFS. The proposed hand-code NCA solves the shortest path and diameter problem. In the experimental evaluation, NCA outperforms other archtectures like GCN or MLP in terms of accuracy and the percentage of complete.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- The proposed hand-code NCA architectures could solve the shortest path and diameter problem in 16x16 and 32x32 maze, better than other baseline architectures, such as MLP or GCN.
- The adversarial data evolution seems to contribute to improve the performance of NCA in both shortest path and diameter problem (Table 6).

### Weaknesses
- The problem that the proposed method could solve is only limited to the pathfinding in the squared-size maze, comapred to the widely-applicable previous works such as Graph Cellular Automata [1], or other neural algorithmic reasoning researches [2, 3, 4]. The proposed archtecture seems highly co-dependent to the squared-size maze.

- Graph Cellular Automata might be a competitive baseline compared to hand-code NCA. GCA may solve the shortest path and diameter problems in square-size maze since they can be interpreted as graphs.

- The trend of the performance is not so consistent among different hidden channel, the number of parameters, and other hyperparameters (i.e. larger network doesn't mean higer performance). There are no explanation about such trends and it seems to require extensive hyperparameter search.


[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14237 

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.04537

[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11142

[4] https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.15659
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Quality
- This paper is well-structured.
- The colors of source and target (and path) in Figure 1 (a) are hard to distinguish.
- It might better include appendix to the main PDF for the readability.

### Clarity
The details of hand-code implementations are only written in Appendix, which make it hard to find the novelty of the architectures. 

### Originality
The neural algorithmic reasoning has been well-studied for a long time, but the relevance to these works are not stated enough. It is not clear whether the hand-code neural implementation of BFS/DFS is an significant contribution to the community.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed hand-code NCA is only limited to the square-size maze problems compared to the more general purpose existing works, which might not be enough contribution to the community. Also,  the comparison with a possibly important baseline, Graph Cellular Automata, is missing. Considering those aspects, I vote for rejection.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
## Summary

The paper proposes manipulating (Neural) Cellular Automata (a.k.a. NCA, [1])  to architecturally align with cellular automata for pathfinding algorithmic problems (BFS / DFS / ShortestPath / Diameter). The paper particularly focuses on path finding in the grid-based mazes domain. Hand-coded NCAs are provided that ‘simulate’ BFS and DFS and another, hand-coded, implementation that combines cellular BFS and DFS to compute graph diameter is also provided. Based on observations when implementing hand-coded NCAs, certain modifications to the original NCA architecture [1] are proposed. Resulting models are compared to baselines -- MLP and GCN [2] (nodes represent maze pos., edges connect traversable positions) and are tested for strong generalisation on larger grids. A number of ablations and an error analysis are also performed (cf. Tables 2-6 main text, Fig.2 Appendix). Results obtained, though sometimes at odds with prior work as the authors note themselves, suggest that NCAs generalise best when the architecture preserves properties that hand-coded solutions possess (e.g. weight sharing/zeroing corners/max-pooling in the convolution weights/etc.).

As stated in the reviewer guide (https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2023/ReviewerGuide), I provide my questions for additional evidence/discussion. Further below I also provide my feedback, which is more long term and may have not directly affected my review.

## Questions

* The authors mention explicitly in the conclusion that “hand-coded models can provide insight into learning more general models”. To what extent is that scalable? E.g. handcoding DFS, a relatively simple algorithm, requires a lot of expert knowledge and usage of fancy activation functions. More complex algorithms may not even be possible to encode.
* If, in the hand-coded NCA, Dijkstra has to wait for DFS, do you have any intuition how the learnable NCA learns to wait? And how often does it learn to wait at all? Diameter results, when tested on strong generalisation, even with adversarial data evolution and other architectural modifications exhibited large standard deviations. (Table 6, bottom right)
* The overall discovery that learnable NCAs can mimic accurately hand-coded NCAs of algorithms is not much surprising to me: e.g. we know algorithmic networks exist (GNNs/Transformers) and hand-coding NCAs is hand-coding an algorithm. What sets apart this approach? Efficiency? -- add experiments on efficiency (but bear in mind graph-oriended hardware also exists). Better generalisation? -- compare to models that generalise well (e.g. [6])

## Feedback for improvement

* It might be often the case (as also questioned above) that we may not be able to find a hand-encoding of an algorithm which we desire to model with a cellular automaton. The authors may strengthen the paper by either discussing what can be performed in such a case, and/or perform experiments where the underlying algorithm is not trivially encodable. One potential option can be a toy shortest path on a pixel grid, where pixel colours denote weights, but no biases (be it architectural improvements, or others) are given to the NCA, apart from possibly using adaptations inspired from the classic black&white shortest path problem.
* Figure 3, which is never referenced in the main text, is a really strong figure. I believe it should be incorporated in the main text. Similarly, an example of what the hand-coded CA automaton matrices look like (as in the Appendix) can also improve understanding of the main text.
* Note, that unless you are aiming for SOTA results, it may not be necessary to compare with GNNs. 
* Regarding writeup, perhaps aim for a bit less text and a bit more visualisations. (E.g. as Figure 3 from the Appendix)
* Tables could also be visualised better (cf. https://people.inf.ethz.ch/markusp/teaching/guides/guide-tables.pdf)

## References (citations also appear further)
[1] Mordvintsev, A., Niklasson, E., & Randazzo, E. (2021). Texture Generation with Neural Cellular Automata. arXiv preprint arXiv:2105.07299.

[2] Kipf, T. N. and Welling, M. (2017). Semi-supervised classification with graph
convolutional networks. In 5th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2017, Toulon, France, April 24-26, 2017, Conference Track Proceedings. OpenReview.net.

[3] Adamatzky, A. I. (1996). Computation of shortest path in cellular automata. Mathematical and Computer Modelling, 23(4), 105-113.

[4] Xu, K., Zhang, M., Li, J., Du, S. S., Kawarabayashi, K. I., & Jegelka, S. (2021, January). How neural networks extrapolate: from feedforward to graph neural networks. In International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

[5] Tang, H., Huang, Z., Gu, J., Lu, B. L., & Su, H. (2020). Towards scale-invariant graph-related problem solving by iterative homogeneous GNNs. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33, 15811-15822

[6] Ibarz, B., Kurin, V., Papamakarios, G., Nikiforou, K., Bennani, M., Csordás, R., ... & Veličković, P. (2022). A Generalist Neural Algorithmic Learner. arXiv preprint arXiv:2209.11142.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Pros
* Cellular automata for algorithmic reasoning seems like an interesting direction to explore
* Architectural decisions are motivated from the fact what the targeted algorithm does, i.e. the paper does not randomly copy/modify an old architecture.
* It is a sound hypothesis that aligning the NCA architecture with the algorithm should lead to improved performance.
* Problem formulation is clear
## Cons
* The first concern is the first contribution of the paper. The paper states that they “develop hand-coded NCAs for the shortest path finding problem”. However, I am able to find works like Adamatzky [3], which seem to implement shortest path finding algorithms, with the difference that they operate on directed+weighted graphs. The grid mazes here correspond to undirected and unweighted graphs. As a GNN researcher,(one that represents an undirected edge with two directed edges) it seems to me that the problem considered here is a subcase of a more general setting and I believe this point should not be stated as a contribution.
* Contrary to the authors, I do NOT find the result at odds with past research. Note that Xu et al. [4] had an explicit section on extrapolation of GNNs. Although mean-aggregating GNNs were not surveyed, analysis showed that max-pooling outweighs sum-pooling.  Similarly, plain GAT/GCN does not generalise well as shown in Tang et al. [5]. (cf. Tables 1-3). It comes as no surprise to me that here GCN underperformed a lot. If you want to compare to a GNN baseline, please pick more appropriate models.
* I find the experimental setup a bit odd:
    * The model’s output is clipped between 0 and 1, but a MSE loss is used. It might be more suitable to consider the output prediction as a binary classification task and train with binary cross entropy. (It may improve performance of ALL models). As it is now, if an NCA after the first iteration mispredicts, and outputs a value that is very large, it can make the iteration ‘explode’, potentially leading to unstable gradients, etc.
    * It is unclear how the accuracy is computed. (State the equation explicitly, please.) Inverse loss, as stated in the text, should still be a positive number, as MSE is a function that is always positive (1/positive=positive). It is also not clear what normalization against all-zero output is. Please elaborate this point.
    * Perhaps MAPE as in Xu et al. is more suitable here as a metric. Alternatively, F1 score could also be used when outputs are either 0 (cell not on shortest path) or 1 (cell on shortest path).
    * There is no `pct. complete` metric for 32x32 grid size. Consider adding the result.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity
* The overall writeup is a bit hard to follow and confusing at times:
    * Terming the hand-coded NCA as ‘neural’ comes confusing at first.
    * similarly, with subscript indexing with (i, j) -- without the appendix visualisations, it was initially unclear where the naming comes from.
    * `sawtooth` is never defined in text. “We used a sawtooth [...]” reads very weird, *when it is without* a reference to the appendix. (Unless referred to, reviewers are not required to read the appendix; https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2023/CallForPapers) People may confuse `sawtooth` with the sawtooth wave from signal processing. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawtooth_wave
    * Not having (or being referred to) visualisations makes reading/understanding the paper a bit difficult.
## Quality
* The overall quality is below the margin of acceptance. Presentation, both in terms of text and in terms of typesetting can be improved. (Please refer to Strengths&Weaknesses for details)
## Originality
* I am not yet convinced of the originality of the proposed approach. In terms of cellular automata it seems it is not the first approach to implement BFS. In terms of algorithmic reasoning/execution it is not the first approach to use NNs for algorithms. It is indeed the first approach to execute algorithms with neural (learnable, that is) cellular automata, but it remained a bit unclear to me what the main benefit of this is, given experiments neither tested efficiency, nor tested against strongly generalising models.
## Reproducibility
* Some minor details are lacking in text but repository with the code is provided, which helps with reproducibility to some extent. The README however contains some TODOs and is unclear how one can load pre-trained models (provided in `runs_eval`), but I do NOT consider this to be a major issue.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the slight overstatement of contributions, confusing writeup at a couple of places and relatively weak evaluation setup, I cannot currently recommend acceptance.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes handcoding NCAs for the shortest path finding problem. They also present an NCA implementation of Depth-First Search (DFS) combining with BFS to address the diameter problem, the longest shortest path between any nodes in the graph. The experiments results show that NCAs work better than GCNs and MLPs in pathfinding problems and hand-coded models can provide good solutions for pathfinding problems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ Paper is well written and easy to read. 
+ The idea of using NCAs for Dijkstra map generation and DFS implementation is interesting. 
+ Hand-code NCAs implementation for Dijkstra map generation, path extraction, and DFS.
+ The experiment results show NCAs are good model for pathfinding problem compared with other baseline models. 
+ Leverage weight sharing technique to reduce the model size while improving the model generalization. 
+ Code is available and clear. 

-	While the work claims to solve two problems (i.e., shortest path and diameter), the experiments result for diameter is not good enough in the test set. 
-	The performance greatly deteriorates when working on the in larger test set. 
-	I suggest adding a comparison experiment for diameter with & without weight sharing even they did in shortest path experiment. 
-	It is not clear if it works on large-scale problems (only 16x16 size for training and 32x32 size for testing in the paper).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written and easy to follow.  
NCA is not a new idea but leveraging NCAs for pathfinding problem is interesting. 
The experiments setting up is easy and clear. The code is available, and the reproducibility of paper is good.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the pathfinding NCAs is an interesting problem and the author implemented NCAs in many sub-tasks of pathfinding, and the experiments show NCAs is better than other baselines in shortest pathfinding, it is still not clear for many aspects, including the mentioned weaknesses. This paper also misses some important analysis. For example, why larger kernel size results in a performance degradation in diameter? I suggest the authors add more ablation studies and clearly explain why and how the parameters (e.g., kernel size) impact on the problems.

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper provides models for Neural Cellular Automata that each learn to perform a pathfinding task in a grid-based domain, i.e. maze traversal.  A neural implementation of BFS is used to find a shortest path, and a combination of BFS and DFS are used to find the diameter.  Favorable are drawn to Graph Convolutional Networks and MLPs, and further improvements are realised with adversarial data generation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The writing is very strong and all points are well-justified.  The main points of the paper are clear and easy to follow.  The reasoning of implementation details in terms of the classical algorithms—for example, the fact that a proper stack implementation requires 5x5 convolutions instead of 3x3—were satisfying.

The biggest issue of the presentation is the lack of architectural diagrams; without a background in NCAs (which I lack), it is difficult to understand, for example, the difference between the NCA and GCN networks.  Additionally, since the authors claim the GCN implementation is "close" to the NCA one, with a GCN substituted for a CNN, the NCA vs. GCN comparison feels more like a CNN vs. GCN comparison.  I would like to see more exposition on these design choices and more elaboration on the core message of the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The quality of the exposition is high overall.  The description of what was done, why it was done, and what the experimental results were, is solid.

Clarity is high when it comes to technical details, but the authors don't clearly explain the significance of their own work.  Are new implementations of NCAs a big step, or a small one?  The broader context is missing, and as a non-NCA expert I have trouble filling it in.

I can't say with certainty, but my sense is that the level of originality is modest.  The "neural implementations" follow the original algorithms so closely that it seems unsurprising that their task performance and generalisation are high.  Since these implementations are not demonstrated to perform well on more than their assigned task, the relevance of these results to the broader community is unclear.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper provides interesting insights on algorithmic alignment in the context of grid-based pathfinding.  And it provides new NCAs for performing two pathfinding tasks, which are well-considered and grounded in the classical algorithms.  However, with no background knowledge in NCAs myself, I cannot easily see the impactfulness of these contributions.

The writing and overall exposition are strong, however, and the ideas are worth thinking about.  I would consider upgrading my score if the paper were augmented with a persuasive argument for its novelty and broader impact.
